title: Rafael and the Asset
premise: Wren Oyelaran, a translator for a doomed peace delegation in the fictional state of Vessania, receives calls on a burner phone from his dead mentor, Elias, whose voice is either a recording, a ghost, or a man still alive and hunted. The phone contains proof that the 'asset' both governments claim to want peace over is actually a stolen ledger of assassinations brokered by officials on all three sides, including Wren's own handler. As an assassin named Corvus closes in and the delegation collapses into pretext for war, Wren must smuggle the truth to a journalist across three borders while deciding whether Elias betrayed him or saved him. In the end Wren trades his own invisibility—and nearly his life—to publish the ledger, exposing his handler but learning Elias chose death to make the phone ring.
about_author: I. M. Kavanagh is the pen name of a former NGO field officer who spent six years interpreting in ceasefire negotiations before turning to fiction. They write thrillers about people whose professions require them to be believed and never seen.

chapters.title: The Go-Bag
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Introduces Wren interpreting at a fractious pre-summit dinner in the capital of Vessania, showing his polished lie—a fabricated family back home—and his packed bag under the bed. He notices his handler, Dreyse, watching him too closely. Emotional beat: controlled unease, the discipline of invisibility beginning to crack.

chapters.title: A Voice That Was Buried
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A burner phone appears in his coat lining; when it rings, Elias—his mentor, officially dead eleven months—speaks four words: 'You were never invisible.' Wren verifies the number exists nowhere. Emotional beat: vertigo and grief reignited; the safe architecture of Wren's life develops its first fault line.

chapters.title: Terms of Interpretation
chapters.summary: Wren's POV interwoven with a short Corvus section. At formal talks, Wren deliberately mistranslates one phrase to buy time, and realizes Dreyse expected it. Meanwhile Corvus arrives in country with a kill list that includes 'the interpreter.' Emotional beat: Wren moves from curiosity to complicity—he has now committed his first act of deception on purpose.

chapters.title: What Elias Left Ringing
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Following the phone's instructions to a locker, he finds a partial ledger: dates, codenames, payments routed through all three delegations' own officials. One entry names Dreyse. Emotional beat: betrayal as physical illness; the peace process reframes as theater staged around a crime.

chapters.title: Dreyse's Kindness
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Dreyse offers Wren a promotion and extraction—an offer that reads as either protection or a test. Wren accepts while hiding the ledger in the one place no one searches: inside his translation notebooks, encoded as glossary entries. Emotional beat: the terror of smiling while dying inside.

chapters.title: Corvus Works
chapters.summary: Corvus's POV. A cold, methodical chapter as Corvus eliminates a courier and reconstructs the phone's chain of custody, narrowing toward the delegation. We see Corvus's own inheritance—a trade passed down like property. Emotional beat: dread through competence; the reader learns how good the hunter is.

chapters.title: The Second Call
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Elias calls again, live this time, and gives Wren a rendezvous—but the call is cut mid-sentence by gunfire Wren can hear. Wren must decide whether the meeting point is rescue or bait. Emotional beat: hope weaponized against him; grief refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: Summit of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The summit opens amid a manufactured border incident; Wren interprets speeches he now knows are scripted lies, and catches a delegate using a codename from the ledger. Emotional beat: moral nausea—the machinery of war running smoothly on rails laid by men in this room.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The rendezvous is a trap; Wren escapes because Corvus was ordered to take him alive, which tells Wren someone wants what's in his head. He burns his apartment and goes dark with the go-bag. Emotional beat: the end of the double life; fear transmuting into resolve.

chapters.title: Three Governments, One Truth
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren maps his options: the journalist Marta Ilic in a neighboring state, a hostile consulate, or silence. Each call he makes is monitored; he uses interpreter tradecraft—dead drops hidden in diplomatic pouches of documents he translates. Emotional beat: loneliness sharpening into ingenuity.

chapters.title: The Handler's Confession
chapters.summary: Dreyse's POV. Dreyse confronts his own role, revealing he helped bury the ledger years ago to protect a career and a country that no longer deserves it. He orders Wren found—not killed. Emotional beat: corruption as slow sediment, power rationalizing itself one compromise at a time.

chapters.title: Border of Salt
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren travels under a dead man's papers through checkpoint country, forced to interpret for a smuggler's crew to pay passage. He decodes another ledger page and finds his own name listed—not as target, but as asset. Emotional beat: identity collapse; the discovery that he was always part of the machine.

chapters.title: Corvus Closes
chapters.summary: Corvus's POV. Corvus corners Wren at a rail yard but hesitates upon seeing the ledger page bearing Corvus's own father's codename among the paid. He lets Wren run. Emotional beat: the assassin's inheritance curdling into doubt; two legacies of violence recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Marta
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reaches journalist Marta Ilic, who tests him brutally—she's been burned by sources before. He passes verification by translating her old article back into the exact dialect errors of its original source. Emotional beat: cautious alliance; the relief of being believed for the first time.

chapters.title: The Delegation Fails
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The summit collapses on schedule; airstrikes are authorized within hours. Dreyse initiates evacuation protocols designed to disappear inconvenient staff—including Wren. Emotional beat: the horror of inevitability; history moving faster than truth.

chapters.title: Everything Translated
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Racing publication deadlines, Wren and Marta authenticate the ledger, discovering the final page: Elias's signature, dated after his death. Elias faked dying to become the ledger's living courier—and the phone was his failsafe. Emotional beat: grief reorganized as understanding; the dead mentor's final lesson.

chapters.title: The Extraction Order
chapters.summary: Dreyse's POV. Dreyse's own superiors turn on him; he realizes he is the next name being cleaned from the list. He makes a desperate choice—contacting Wren not to stop the story but to survive it. Emotional beat: power devouring its own; the corruptor corrupted.

chapters.title: Safe House, Unsafe Silence
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Holed up with Marta awaiting transmission, Wren endures a siege as Corvus—now off-script and unpaid—arrives not to kill but to demand the page naming his father. Emotional beat: siege tension; enemies negotiating over shared damage.

chapters.title: Transmission
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Under fire, Marta transmits the ledger to networks on three continents. Corvus holds the door, choosing his side at last. Dreyse arrives and takes a bullet meant for Wren, surviving long enough to confirm everything on record. Emotional beat: climax—sacrifice converting secrecy into public fact.

chapters.title: Aftermath in Three Languages
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The story detonates globally; inquiries open; the war stalls for lack of willing liars. Wren testifies via video from hiding, his real name spoken aloud for the first time in years. Emotional beat: exposure as both wound and liberation; invisibility surrendered deliberately.

chapters.title: The Last Call
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Months later, the burner rings once more. It is a lawyer: Elias is truly dead now, and left Wren an inheritance—nothing material, only a recorded message and the choice of what to do with a second, unopened ledger. Emotional beat: mourning completed; inheritance as responsibility rather than property.

chapters.title: Visible
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren unpacks the go-bag at last, keeps the notebooks, and begins teaching interpretation to young refugees—teaching them to be heard, not hidden. The final image: Wren speaking in his own voice, untranslated. Emotional beat: resolution; memory honored, power answered with witness.
